claim: Urodynamic status must interact with arousal and attentional processes so that voiding occurs under appropriate conditions.
source: Urodynamic status must interact with arousal and attentional processes so that voiding occurs under appropriate conditions.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that frames the research question and is based on established understanding of micturition physiology.

claim: PMC neurons had homogeneous firing patterns, characterized by tonic activity and phasic bursts that were temporally associated with distinct phases of the micturition cycle.
source: PMC neurons had homogeneous firing patterns, characterized by tonic activity and phasic bursts that were temporally associated with distinct phases of the micturition cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings from PMC neurons during cystometry as described in the Results section.

claim: LC and cortical activation became synchronized 20-30 s prior to micturition.
source: LC and cortical activation became synchronized 20-30 s prior to micturition.
evidence: This is supported by simultaneous recordings from LC neurons and mPFC during cystometry experiments.

claim: During the pre-micturition interval, a theta oscillation developed in the LC.
source: During this pre-micturition interval, a theta oscillation developed in the LC, the mPFC desynchronized and LC-mPFC coherence increased in the theta frequency range.
evidence: This is supported by LFP recordings and spectral analysis showing theta oscillations in LC during the pre-micturition period.

claim: During the pre-micturition interval, the mPFC desynchronized.
source: During this pre-micturition interval, a theta oscillation developed in the LC, the mPFC desynchronized and LC-mPFC coherence increased in the theta frequency range.
evidence: This is supported by LFP recordings showing decreased power across frequencies in mPFC during pre-micturition period.

claim: LC-mPFC coherence increased in the theta frequency range during the pre-micturition interval.
source: During this pre-micturition interval, a theta oscillation developed in the LC, the mPFC desynchronized and LC-mPFC coherence increased in the theta frequency range.
evidence: This is supported by coherence analysis between LC and mPFC LFP recordings.

claim: The temporal offset between the shift in LC-mPFC network activity and micturition may allow time to disengage from ongoing behaviors unrelated to micturition and initiate specific voiding behaviors.
source: The temporal offset between the shift in LC-mPFC network activity and micturition may allow time to disengage from ongoing behaviors unrelated to micturition and initiate specific voiding behaviors so that micturition occurs in environmentally and socially appropriate conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal relationship observed in the data, representing a speculative functional explanation.

claim: In some species micturition is integral to social communication, for example, with regard to sexual status and social rank.
source: In some species micturition is integral to social communication, for example, with regard to sexual status and social rank (Ralls, 1971; Desjardins et al., 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bladder filling should increase arousal and shift the focus of attention before pressure reaches the micturition threshold.
source: For example, bladder filling should increase arousal and shift the focus of attention before pressure reaches the micturition threshold so that ongoing behavior is suspended and voiding behavior is initiated prior to the passage of urine.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the functional requirements of micturition control based on established knowledge.

claim: A lack of coordination between voiding behaviors and micturition characterizes dysfunctional voiding syndromes, such as enuresis.
source: A lack of coordination between voiding behaviors and micturition characterizes dysfunctional voiding syndromes, such as enuresis that can occur both in children and older adults (Torrens and Collins, 1975; Nevéus, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: The pontine micturition center (PMC) is central to a circuit that is positioned to coordinate neurobehavioral and visceral limbs of micturition.
source: The pontine micturition center (PMC) is central to a circuit that is positioned to coordinate neurobehavioral and visceral limbs of micturition (Valentino et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The PMC is proposed to function as an all or none switch, whereby the neurons become activated at some threshold pressure and engage the descending limb that initiates bladder contraction.
source: Through its projections to lumbosacral preganglionic neurons that regulate the parasympathetic innervation of the detrusor, the PMC is proposed to function as an all or none switch, whereby the neurons become activated at some threshold pressure and engage the descending limb that initiates bladder contraction (de Groat, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A population of spinal-projecting PMC neurons are retrogradely labeled from both the lumbosacral spinal cord and the pontine noradrenergic nucleus locus coeruleus (LC).
source: We identified a population of spinal-projecting PMC neurons that are retrogradely labeled from both the lumbosacral spinal cord and the pontine noradrenergic nucleus locus coeruleus (LC) (Valentino et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: The LC has a widely distributed axonal network that extensively innervates the forebrain and particularly the cortex where norepinephrine serves as a neuromodulator of cortical activity.
source: The LC has a widely distributed axonal network that extensively innervates the forebrain and particularly the cortex where norepinephrine serves as a neuromodulator of cortical activity (Swanson and Hartman, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: Selective pharmacological or optogenetic activation of LC neurons or activation using Gs-linked DREADDS is sufficient to produce cortical electroencephalographic (EEG) activation indicative of arousal.
source: Selective pharmacological or optogenetic activation of LC neurons or activation using Gs-linked DREADDS is sufficient to produce cortical electroencephalographic (EEG) activation indicative of arousal (Berridge and Foote, 1991; Carter et al., 2010; Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: LC neurons are activated by bladder and colonic distention and this is temporally linked to cortical EEG activation.
source: Notably, LC neurons are activated by bladder and colonic distention and this is temporally linked to cortical EEG activation (Elam et al., 1986; Page et al., 1992; Lechner et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: LC activation is thought to reset attentional networks to shift the focus of attention to salient stimuli.
source: In addition to increasing arousal in response to salient stimuli, LC activation is thought to reset attentional networks to shift the focus of attention to salient stimuli (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981a; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Bouret and Sara, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Single unit activity was recorded from 36 PMC neurons from three rats during in vivo cystometry.
source: Single unit activity was recorded from 36 PMC neurons from three rats during in vivo cystometry.
evidence: This describes the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: The pattern of PMC neuronal discharge was relatively homogeneous across all three rats.
source: Whether depicted as the raw waveform trace (Figure 1C) or rate (Figure 1D), the pattern of PMC neuronal discharge was relatively homogeneous and this was true across all three rats (Figures 1C, D and 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: In all rats, PMC neurons discharged during micturition until bladder pressure decreased to zero and the bladder was empty.
source: Consistent with this, in all rats, PMC neurons discharged during micturition until bladder pressure decreased to zero and the bladder was empty (Figures 1C, D and 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: All PMC neurons exhibited burst activity at different times with respect to micturition.
source: All PMC neurons also exhibited burst activity at different times with respect to micturition (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by burst analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: Post-micturition bursts averaging 28 ± 1 Hz frequency and 606 ± 66 ms in duration occurred within the 20 s period following micturition.
source: This was particularly apparent within the 20 s period following micturition during which bursts averaging 28 ± 1 Hz frequency and 606 ± 66 ms in duration occurred (Table 1, Figures 1C, 2A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative burst analysis data.

claim: Post-micturition bursts were sometimes associated with a very small, transient increase in bladder pressure.
source: These post-micturition bursts were sometimes associated with a very small, transient increase in bladder pressure (Figure 2A asterisks).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In all PMC cells similar bursts (28 ± 2 Hz, 432 ± 35 ms duration) occurred regularly during inter-micturition intervals when bladder pressure was low.
source: Notably, in all PMC cells similar bursts (28 ± 2 Hz, 432 ± 35 ms duration) occurred regularly during inter-micturition intervals when bladder pressure was low (Table 1, Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative burst analysis data.

claim: Burst activity was rare during the pre-micturition period (20 s prior to micturition).
source: Burst activity was rare during the pre-micturition period (20 s prior to micturition).
evidence: This claim is supported by burst analysis data in Table 1 showing only 0.3 ± 0.1 bursts during pre-micturition.

claim: Some PMC cells were distinguished by tonic discharge between bursts.
source: Notably, some cells were distinguished by tonic discharge between bursts (Figure 1C, first and third cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: LC neuronal activity was recorded from 51 neurons of 4 rats.
source: LC neuronal activity was recorded from 51 neurons of 4 rats.
evidence: This describes the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: LC neurons were spontaneously active throughout the recordings although discharge rate fluctuated with the micturition cycle.
source: As described in previous studies in unanesthetized rats (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981a), LC neurons were spontaneously active throughout the recordings although discharge rate fluctuated with the micturition cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and comparison to previous literature.

claim: LC neurons consistently increased their discharge rate 10–30 s prior to micturition and this activation ceased with micturition.
source: In contrast to PMC neurons, LC neurons consistently increased their discharge rate 10–30 s prior to micturition and this activation ceased with micturition (Figure 3A,B,C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The distribution of latencies between significant LC activation and micturition ranged between 0 and 65 s with most cells having a latency between 10–30 s.
source: The distribution of latencies between significant LC activation and micturition ranged between 0 and 65 s with most cells having a latency between 10–30 s (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The temporal relationship between LC activation, PMC neuronal activation and micturition argued against the hypothesis that PMC neurons drive LC neurons prior to micturition because LC activation preceded PMC neuronal activation.
source: Notably, the temporal relationship between LC activation, PMC neuronal activation and micturition in this particular case argued against the hypothesis that PMC neurons drive LC neurons prior to micturition because LC activation preceded PMC neuronal activation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal relationships observed in the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The LC neuronal activation, occurring 10–30 s prior to micturition, was temporally correlated with mPFC desynchronization.
source: The LC neuronal activation, occurring 10–30 s prior to micturition, was temporally correlated with mPFC desynchronization (Figure 5A1, A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simultaneous recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Simultaneous local field potential recordings (LFP) in LC and mPFC demonstrate a shift from low frequency activity at baseline to a prominent theta oscillation in the LC during the pre-micturition period.
source: Simultaneous local field potential recordings (LFP) in LC and mPFC demonstrate a shift from low frequency activity at baseline (e.g., Figure 5B1, 0–47 s) to a prominent theta oscillation in the LC during the pre-micturition period (e.g., Figure 5B1, 47–77 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP data shown in Figure 5B1.

claim: The prominent theta oscillation in the LC during the pre-micturition period was accompanied by a desynchronization of the mPFC.
source: This was accompanied by a desynchronization of the mPFC (Figure 5A2, B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Although the mPFC LFP magnitude was small during the 30 s period prior to micturition relative to the preceding baseline interval, there was still evidence of a theta oscillation in the mPFC during this time as well.
source: Interestingly, although the mPFC LFP magnitude was small during the 30 s period prior to micturition relative to the preceding baseline interval, there was still evidence of a theta oscillation in the mPFC during this time as well (white arrowheads in Figure 5B2, Figure 6B, cf., red and black lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP data shown in Figures 5B2 and 6B.

claim: LC activity recorded from 60 to 30 s before micturition shifted from mixed low frequency activity to a prominent theta oscillation occurring 30–0 s before micturition.
source: Thus, LC activity recorded from 60 to 30 s before micturition shifted from mixed low frequency activity to a prominent theta oscillation occurring 30–0 s before micturition.
evidence: This claim is supported by power spectrum analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The mPFC power spectrum shifted from high amplitude, low frequency activity (0–5 Hz) to much lower amplitude oscillations and a decrease of power in all frequencies, characteristic of desynchronization.
source: In concert, the mPFC power spectrum shifted from high amplitude, low frequency activity (0–5 Hz) to much lower amplitude oscillations and a decrease of power in all frequencies, characteristic of desynchronization.
evidence: This claim is supported by power spectrum analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: An increase in coherence between the LC and mPFC in the theta frequency characterized the pre-micturition interval.
source: An increase in coherence between the LC and mPFC in the theta frequency characterized this pre-micturition interval (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by coherence analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The change in LC and mPFC LFP activity reverted with bladder emptying.
source: This change in LC and mPFC LFP activity reverted with bladder emptying (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 5.

claim: The present findings demonstrated a temporal offset between LC neuronal activation and micturition during which a theta oscillation develops in the LC, LC-mPFC coherence is increased and the mPFC becomes desynchronized.
source: Importantly, the findings demonstrated a temporal offset between LC neuronal activation and micturition during which a theta oscillation develops in the LC, LC-mPFC coherence is increased and the mPFC becomes desynchronized.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main experimental findings.

claim: These changes in the LC-mPFC network activity may facilitate the initiation of voiding behaviors prior to micturition by increasing arousal and shifting attention towards visceral demands.
source: These changes in the LC-mPFC network activity may facilitate the initiation of voiding behaviors prior to micturition by increasing arousal and shifting attention towards visceral demands.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed network changes.

claim: In vivo cystometry does not mimic natural micturition cycles, which would be longer in the absence of steady bladder infusion.
source: In vivo cystometry was used to monitor and regulate micturition cycles. However, it does not mimic natural micturition cycles, which would be longer in the absence of steady bladder infusion.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The multiwire recording technique allows for sampling activity from multiple neurons within the same nucleus, but the results are inevitably biased toward activity that the wires can record from and that can be reliably discriminated.
source: Although the multiwire recording technique allows for sampling activity from multiple neurons within the same nucleus, the results are inevitably biased toward activity that the wires can record from and that can be reliably discriminated.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The PMC is neurochemically heterogeneous.
source: This may be a particular problem for PMC which is neurochemically heterogeneous (Sutin and Jacobowitz, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The LC is relatively homogeneous in the rat.
source: This is less of a caveat for the LC, which is relatively homogeneous in the rat (Aston-Jones et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Most previous studies of PMC neuronal activity with relation to bladder pressure were done in anesthetized rats or cats with the bladder distended under isotonic conditions.
source: Most previous studies of PMC neuronal activity with relation to bladder pressure were done in anesthetized rats or cats with the bladder distended under isotonic conditions such that reflex contractions would occur (Willette et al., 1988; Tanaka et al., 2003; de Groat and Wickens, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Three general neuronal types were identified in anesthetized animals: neurons that discharge before and during reflex bladder contractions, neurons that are inhibited during contractions and active between contractions, and neurons that fire transiently at the beginning of the contractions.
source: Three general neuronal types were identified in these conditions, neurons that discharge before and during reflex bladder contractions, neurons that are inhibited during contractions and active between contractions and neurons that fire transiently at the beginning of the contractions.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies cited in the text.

claim: The majority of recorded neurons in anesthetized studies were of the second type (inhibited during contractions and active between contractions).
source: The majority of recorded neurons in those studies were of the second type.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies cited in the text.

claim: One study recorded activity throughout the pons and medulla during cystometry in the absence of anesthesia in the decerebrate cat.
source: One study recorded activity throughout the pons and medulla during cystometry in the absence of anesthesia in the decerebrate cat (Sugaya et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the decerebrate cat study, nearly all neurons that were inhibited during bladder contraction were ventral to the region corresponding to the PMC, whereas most neurons within the PMC were activated during bladder contraction.
source: Notably, in that study the mapping of these neuronal types demonstrated that nearly all neurons that were inhibited during bladder contraction were ventral to the region corresponding to the PMC, whereas most neurons within the PMC were activated during bladder contraction.
evidence: This claim is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claim: The present study is unique in recording single unit activity from the PMC in the intact unanesthetized and freely moving rat during cystometry.
source: The present study is unique in recording single unit activity from the PMC in the intact unanesthetized and freely moving rat during cystometry.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study's methodology.

claim: PMC neurons recorded in this study were homogeneous in the temporal correlation of their discharge pattern with the micturition cycle and resembled the previously described excitatory neurons.
source: PMC neurons recorded in this study were homogeneous in the temporal correlation of their discharge pattern with the micturition cycle and resembled the previously described excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous literature.

claim: The present results are consistent with recent studies using photometry to measure the calcium currents in genetically-identified CRF-PMC neurons in unanesthetized mice during cystometry.
source: Notably, the present results are consistent with recent studies using photometry to measure the calcium currents in genetically-identified CRF-PMC neurons in unanesthetized mice during cystometry (Hou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous literature.

claim: Studies using photometry demonstrated a signal that was most prominent coincident with and up to 10 s after micturition.
source: These studies demonstrated a signal that was most prominent coincident with and up to 10 s after micturition.
evidence: This claim is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claim: CRF is co-localized with glutamate in PMC neurons.
source: However, CRF is co-localized with glutamate in PMC neurons (Hou et al., 2016) and evidence suggests that CRF is inhibitory in this pathway and may counteract the excitatory effects of glutamate neurotransmission (Pavcovich and Valentino, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Evidence suggests that CRF is inhibitory in the PMC pathway and may counteract the excitatory effects of glutamate neurotransmission.
source: However, CRF is co-localized with glutamate in PMC neurons (Hou et al., 2016) and evidence suggests that CRF is inhibitory in this pathway and may counteract the excitatory effects of glutamate neurotransmission (Pavcovich and Valentino, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Higher frequency bursts that favor neuropeptide release could be a mechanism for switching the function of the nucleus from one that facilitates active emptying to one that facilitates storage by countering detrusor contraction.
source: Higher frequency bursts that favor neuropeptide release could be a mechanism for switching the function of the nucleus from one that facilitates active emptying to one that facilitates storage by countering detrusor contraction.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of burst patterns.

claim: Rat LC neurons are relatively homogeneous in that they are all noradrenergic and have similar electrophysiological properties.
source: Rat LC neurons are relatively homogeneous in that they are all noradrenergic and have similar electrophysiological properties (Aston-Jones et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A characteristic property of LC neurons of both anesthetized and unanesthetized rats is their activation by salient sensory stimuli of all modalities.
source: A characteristic property of LC neurons of both anesthetized and unanesthetized rats is their activation by salient sensory stimuli of all modalities (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: LC neurons are also activated by diverse physiological stimuli including hypotension and non-noxious distention of the bladder or colon.
source: LC neurons are also activated by diverse physiological stimuli including hypotension and non-noxious distention of the bladder or colon (Elam et al., 1985; Elam et al., 1986; Valentino and Wehby, 1988; Page et al., 1992; Lechner et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LC neurons become tonically activated approximately 20 s prior to micturition and in most cases before the steady pressure rise to micturition threshold.
source: In the present study, LC neuronal recordings during in vivo cystometry in unanesthetized rats revealed an exquisite sensitivity of LC neurons in that they become tonically activated approximately 20 s prior to micturition and in most cases before the steady pressure rise to micturition threshold (Figures 3 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: LC activation by bladder stimuli may be a response to bladder wall stretching rather than an increase in intravesicular pressure.
source: Possibly, this is a response to bladder wall stretching rather than an increase in intravesicular pressure.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism of LC activation.

claim: Previous lesion studies provided evidence that LC activation by colonic distention was mediated by PMC.
source: Previous lesion studies provided evidence that LC activation by colonic distention was mediated by PMC but bladder distention was not examined in that study (Rouzade-Dominguez et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Another route by which the LC could receive bladder information is through the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG).
source: Another route by which the LC could receive bladder information is through the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: Anterogradely labeled vlPAG fibers innervate both PMC and the rostromedial peri-LC and synaptically contact LC dendrites in this region.
source: Anterogradely labeled vlPAG fibers innervate both PMC and the rostromedial peri-LC and synaptically contact LC dendrites in this region (Bajic et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: The PAG could regulate both the LC and the PMC in response to bladder related stimuli.
source: The PAG then could regulate both the LC and the PMC in response to bladder related stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on anatomical connectivity.

claim: The LC-norepinephrine system densely innervates the mPFC and modulates its activity and executive functions.
source: The LC-norepinephrine system densely innervates the mPFC and modulates its activity and executive functions (Arnsten and Li, 2005; Arnsten, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Regionally selective pharmacological activation of the LC or activation using Designer Receptor Exclusively Activated by Designer Drug (DREADD) technology produces a desynchronization of the cortical EEG (an arousal response).
source: Regionally selective pharmacological activation of the LC or activation using Designer Receptor Exclusively Activated by Designer Drug (DREADD) technology produces a desynchronization of the cortical EEG (an arousal response) (Berridge and Foote, 1991; Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: LC activation by certain stimuli is necessary for their ability to elicit cortical arousal.
source: Moreover, LC activation by certain stimuli is necessary for their ability to elicit cortical arousal (Valentino et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: LC activation is necessary for bladder distention to elicit cortical arousal.
source: This includes bladder distention produced by injection of saline in anesthetized rats (Page et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The present results identified an important temporal relationship between LC activity, mPFC activity and bladder pressure, with LC and cortical activation being synchronized to occur approximately 20 s prior to micturition.
source: The present results identified an important temporal relationship between LC activity, mPFC activity and bladder pressure, with LC and cortical activation being synchronized to occur approximately 20 s prior to micturition.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main experimental findings.

claim: During the pre-micturition interval when LC neuronal activity is elevated, network activity shifts from low frequency oscillations to a prominent theta oscillation.
source: The examination of network activity in the LC and between the LC and mPFC revealed that during this pre-micturition interval when LC neuronal activity is elevated, network activity shifts from low frequency oscillations to a prominent theta oscillation.
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis of LFP data.

claim: During the pre-micturition interval, mPFC activity desynchronizes as characterized by a decreased power in all frequencies but LC-mPFC coherence, specifically in the theta frequency, is increased.
source: At the same time mPFC activity desynchronizes as characterized by a decreased power in all frequencies but LC-mPFC coherence, specifically in the theta frequency, is increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral and coherence analysis of LFP data.

claim: The network shift that is temporally offset from micturition may be a neural code to increase arousal and reset behavior prior to micturition so that voiding occurs in appropriate environments.
source: This network shift that is temporally offset from micturition may be a neural code to increase arousal and reset behavior prior to micturition so that voiding occurs in appropriate environments.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed network changes.

claim: Signals arising from bladder-related pathology could impact on cortical function through the same networks that relay normal bladder signals to the cortex.
source: Just as normal bladder signals are relayed to the cortex, signals arising from bladder-related pathology could impact on cortical function through these same networks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the identified neural pathways.

claim: Partial bladder outlet obstruction produces an abnormal urodynamic pattern that is associated with robust changes in cortical network activity.
source: Consistent with this, partial bladder outlet obstruction produces an abnormal urodynamic pattern that is associated with robust changes in cortical network activity (Rickenbacher et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Partial bladder outlet obstruction is characterized by frequent non-micturition contractions that are temporally correlated with persistent cortical theta oscillations.
source: This condition is characterized by frequent non-micturition contractions that are temporally correlated with persistent cortical theta oscillations.
evidence: This claim is based on previous work cited in the text.

claim: Selective lesion of LC-forebrain projections using the toxin, DSP-4, prevented the cortical changes without affecting the abnormal urodynamics in partial bladder outlet obstruction.
source: Selective lesion of LC-forebrain projections using the toxin, DSP-4, prevented the cortical changes without affecting the abnormal urodynamics.
evidence: This claim is based on previous experimental work cited in the text.

claim: The LC-cortical network is important in communicating bladder status to the cortex.
source: This underscores the importance of the LC-cortical network in communicating bladder status to the cortex and suggests that dysregulation of this network could be a prominent signature of underlying bladder pathology.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation of the LC-cortical network could be a prominent signature of underlying bladder pathology.
source: This underscores the importance of the LC-cortical network in communicating bladder status to the cortex and suggests that dysregulation of this network could be a prominent signature of underlying bladder pathology.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: Female adult Sprague-Dawley rats were used as subjects.
source: Female adult Sprague-Dawley rats (Charles River, Wilmington, MA) were maintained in a temperature and light controlled environment (20°C, 12 hr light-dark cycle, lights on at 0700 hr) with food and water available ad libitum.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: LC neurons were tentatively identified during recording by their spontaneous discharge rates (0.5–5 Hz), entirely positive, notched waveforms (2–3 ms duration), and biphasic excitatory–inhibitory responses to contralateral hindpaw or tail pinch.
source: LC neurons were tentatively identified during recording by their spontaneous discharge rates (0.5–5 Hz), entirely positive, notched waveforms (2–3 ms duration), and biphasic excitatory–inhibitory responses to contralateral hindpaw or tail pinch.
evidence: This describes the electrophysiological criteria used to identify LC neurons.

claim: Sterile saline was continuously infused at 100 μl/min through the bladder catheter during cystometry.
source: Sterile saline was continuously infused (100 μl/min) through the bladder catheter while urodynamic endpoints, including bladder pressure and the timing of micturition were recorded on-line for 1 hr using cystometry equipment (Medical Associates, St. Albans, VT) and software (Cystometry Analysis Software, SOF-522, Catamount R and D, St. Albans, VT).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA indicated significant differences between the two time periods for LC power (F(1,742)=221, p<0.0001).
source: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA with frequency as the repeated measure indicated significant differences between the two time periods for LC power (F(1,742)=221, p<0.0001), PFC power (F(1,742)=671, p<0.0001 and LC-PFC coherence (F(1,2940) = 121, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA indicated significant differences between the two time periods for PFC power (F(1,742)=671, p<0.0001).
source: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA with frequency as the repeated measure indicated significant differences between the two time periods for LC power (F(1,742)=221, p<0.0001), PFC power (F(1,742)=671, p<0.0001 and LC-PFC coherence (F(1,2940) = 121, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA indicated significant differences between the two time periods for LC-PFC coherence (F(1,2940) = 121, p<0.001).
source: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA with frequency as the repeated measure indicated significant differences between the two time periods for LC power (F(1,742)=221, p<0.0001), PFC power (F(1,742)=671, p<0.0001 and LC-PFC coherence (F(1,2940) = 121, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The PMC projects to lumbosacral preganglionic neurons that regulate the parasympathetic innervation of the detrusor.
source: Through its projections to lumbosacral preganglionic neurons that regulate the parasympathetic innervation of the detrusor, the PMC is proposed to function as an all or none switch, whereby the neurons become activated at some threshold pressure and engage the descending limb that initiates bladder contraction (de Groat, 2006).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by citation.

claim: The PMC could coordinate visceral and neurobehavioral limbs of the micturition reflex through collateral projections to the LC and spinal cord.
source: Thus, through collateral projections to the LC and spinal cord based on dual retrograde labeling, the PMC could coordinate visceral and neurobehavioral limbs of the micturition reflex.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical findings cited in the text.

claim: After the first micturition cycle, subsequent cycles in rats became regular, with bladder pressure gradually increasing to a peak, at which point micturition occurred and bladder pressure fell to 0 mm Hg.

evidence: This describes the observed pattern of micturition cycles during cystometry.

claim: Most PMC neurons increased their discharge rate during micturition and no recorded neurons were inhibited at this time.
